claim: Transverse (T)-tubules make up a specialized network of tubulated muscle cell membranes involved in excitation-contraction coupling for power of contraction.
source: Transverse (T)-tubules make-up a specialized network of tubulated muscle cell membranes involved in excitation-contraction coupling for power of contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T-tubule structure and function in muscle cells.

claim: Autophagy is upregulated with T-tubule disassembly in Drosophila abdominal muscles during metamorphosis.
source: Here, we show that autophagy is both upregulated with and required for progression through T-tubule disassembly stages.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased autophagy markers coinciding with T-tubule disassembly.

claim: Autophagy is required for progression through T-tubule disassembly stages.
source: Here, we show that autophagy is both upregulated with and required for progression through T-tubule disassembly stages.
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic disruption experiments showing that blocking autophagy prevents T-tubule remodeling.

claim: Rab2 has a conserved function in autophagic clearance.
source: Along with known mediators of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, our screens uncovered an unexpected shared role for Rab2 with a broadly conserved function in autophagic clearance.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from both Drosophila and mammalian cells showing Rab2 function in autophagy.

claim: Rab2 localizes to autophagosomes.
source: Rab2 localizes to autophagosomes and binds to HOPS complex members, suggesting a direct role in autophagosome tethering/fusion.
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data showing colocalization of Rab2 with autophagosome markers.

claim: Rab2 binds to HOPS complex members.
source: Rab2 localizes to autophagosomes and binds to HOPS complex members, suggesting a direct role in autophagosome tethering/fusion.
evidence: The manuscript presents co-immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between Rab2 and HOPS complex components.

claim: Rab2 has a direct role in autophagosome tethering/fusion.
source: Rab2 localizes to autophagosomes and binds to HOPS complex members, suggesting a direct role in autophagosome tethering/fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization and binding data, combined with the phenotype of Rab2 depletion.

claim: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) and T-tubules are membranous organelles involved in excitation-contraction coupling.
source: The power of contraction, however, requires synchronous sarcomere function under control of the 'excitation-contraction coupling' system that includes two membranous organelles, the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) and Transverse (T)-tubules (Al-Qusairi and Laporte, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: T-tubule membrane network invaginates radially inward in a repeated pattern at each sarcomere.
source: The T-tubule membrane network is continuous with the muscle cell plasma membrane, with tubulated membranes that invaginate radially inward in a repeated pattern at each sarcomere.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T-tubule organization.

claim: Neuromuscular action potentials are transmitted along the muscle T-tubule membrane to the SR junction, triggering coordinated SR Ca2+ release and synchronous sarcomere contractions.
source: With excitation-contraction coupling, neuromuscular action potentials are transmitted along the muscle T-tubule membrane to the SR junction, or dyad/triad, triggering coordinated SR Ca2+ release and synchronous sarcomere contractions (Al-Qusairi and Laporte, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about excitation-contraction coupling, cited from the literature.

claim: Formation of organized T-tubule membranes is critical for muscle function.
source: Formation of organized T-tubule membranes is thus critical for muscle function (Takeshima et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: The extent and mechanisms of T-tubule remodeling remain largely unknown.
source: However, the extent and mechanisms of T-tubule remodeling remain largely unknown, in part due to challenges with observing T-tubule membrane network dynamics within intact mammalian myofibers.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In mouse skeletal muscle, mostly longitudinal tubular membranes initially present in embryonic muscle are remodeled postnatally with expansion to predominantly transversal tubular elements.
source: In mouse skeletal muscle, mostly longitudinal tubular membranes initially present in embryonic muscle are remodeled postnatally with expansion to predominantly transversal tubular elements (Takekura et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Both longitudinal and transversal T-tubule elements are maintained in adult mammalian cardiac muscle.
source: In contrast, both longitudinal and transversal T-tubule elements are maintained in adult mammalian cardiac muscle (Brette and Orchard, 2003) and in insect muscles (Razzaq et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Both longitudinal and transversal T-tubule elements are maintained in insect muscles.
source: In contrast, both longitudinal and transversal T-tubule elements are maintained in adult mammalian cardiac muscle (Brette and Orchard, 2003) and in insect muscles (Razzaq et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Relatively few molecular factors are known to shape the T-tubule network, all of which encode for membrane-associated functions (CAV3, DYSF, BIN1/Amph2, MTM1, DNM2).
source: Relatively few molecular factors are known to shape the T-tubule network, and perhaps not surprisingly, all of which so far encode for membrane-associated functions (CAV3, DYSF, BIN1/Amph2, MTM1, DNM2) (Butler et al., 1997; Hnia et al., 2012; Lek et al., 2012; Morlot and Roux, 2013; Tang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from multiple literature sources.

claim: Mutations in CAV3, DYSF, BIN1/Amph2, MTM1, and DNM2 are associated with human myopathy and/or cardiomyopathy with T-tubule disorganization.
source: Mutations in each also are associated with human myopathy and/or cardiomyopathy with T-tubule disorganization (Bashir et al., 1998; Betz et al., 2001; Bitoun et al., 2005; Laporte et al., 1996; Liu et al., 1998; Minetti et al., 1998; Nicot et al., 2007), pointing to the critical importance of membrane-mediated mechanisms to maintain the T-tubule membrane network.
evidence: This is cited from multiple literature sources.

claim: The BIN1 BAR-domain protein has a conserved function involved in membrane tubulation required for T-tubule formation.
source: The BIN1 BAR-domain protein has a conserved function involved in membrane tubulation required for T-tubule formation that was first described for the single Drosophila homolog, Amphiphysin (Lee et al., 2002b; Razzaq et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The amph null mutant flies lack transversal T-tubule element membranes in myofibers at all developmental stages.
source: The amph null mutant flies lack transversal T-tubule element membranes in myofibers at all developmental stages, corresponding with both larval and adult mobility defects (Razzaq et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The myotubularin (mtm) fly homolog is required only at later stages in development for T-tubule remodeling.
source: In contrast, the myotubularin (mtm) fly homolog of mammalian MTM1/MTMR2/MTMR1 subfamily of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate phosphatases is required only at later stages in development for T-tubule remodeling.
evidence: This is based on cited literature and experimental observations.

claim: mtm loss of function has no obvious effects on larval muscle T-tubule organization or function.
source: While mtm loss of function has no obvious effects on larval muscle T-tubule organization or function, mtm-depleted post-larval stage muscles lack transversal T-tubule membranes with adult mobility defects in eclosion and flight (Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: mtm-depleted post-larval stage muscles lack transversal T-tubule membranes with adult mobility defects in eclosion and flight.
source: While mtm loss of function has no obvious effects on larval muscle T-tubule organization or function, mtm-depleted post-larval stage muscles lack transversal T-tubule membranes with adult mobility defects in eclosion and flight (Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Distinct mechanisms are involved in T-tubule formation (amph-dependent) versus maintenance/remodeling (amph- and mtm-dependent).
source: Together, the amph and mtm mutant conditions that both lack transversal T-tubule elements in post-larval stage muscle yet different early development requirements underscores that distinct mechanisms are involved in T-tubule formation (amph-dependent) versus maintenance/remodeling (amph- and mtm-dependent).
evidence: This is inferred from the different phenotypes of amph and mtm mutants.

claim: Drosophila dorsal internal oblique muscles (IOMs) are essential for adult eclosion.
source: In Drosophila, a set of larval body wall muscles that persist as viable pupal abdominal muscles, called dorsal internal oblique muscles (IOMs), are essential for adult eclosion (Kimura and Truman, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Changes in IOM cell size and myofibril content occur during metamorphosis.
source: During metamorphosis, changes in IOM cell size and myofibril content have been noted (Kuleesha et al., 2014, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Wildtype IOMs undergo dramatic cortical and membrane remodeling with costamere integrin adhesion complex disassembly and reassembly at discrete pupal stages.
source: We previously showed that wildtype IOMs undergo dramatic cortical and membrane remodeling with costamere integrin adhesion complex disassembly and reassembly at discrete pupal stages (Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: mtm-depleted IOMs exhibited persistent disassembly or a block in reassembly of integrin costameres along with the loss of transversal T-tubule membranes at late pupal stages, but without any precocious cell death.
source: In contrast, the mtm-depleted IOMs exhibited persistent disassembly or a block in reassembly of integrin costameres along with the loss of transversal T-tubule membranes at late pupal stages, but without any precocious cell death (Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: mtm-depleted IOMs accumulate endosomal-like membranes decorated with integrin and T-tubule markers, Amph and Discs large (Dlg1).
source: A striking feature in the mtm-depleted IOMs was the accumulation of endosomal-like membranes decorated with integrin and T-tubule markers, Amph and Discs large (Dlg1, a PDZ protein).
evidence: This is based on observations from previous work.

claim: T-tubule membranes may undergo disassembly-reassembly with normal myofiber remodeling, including the delivery of disassembled T-tubule membrane into an endomembrane trafficking pathway.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that T-tubule membranes may undergo disassembly-reassembly with normal myofiber remodeling, including the delivery of disassembled T-tubule membrane into an endomembrane trafficking pathway.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: There are over sixty Rabs in humans and thirty in flies.
source: Membrane trafficking relies on the large family of Rab GTPases, with over sixty Rabs in humans and thirty in flies (Klöpper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) convert specific inactive GDP-bound Rabs to an active GTP-bound form.
source: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) convert specific inactive GDP-bound Rabs to an active GTP-bound form.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rab GTPase regulation.

claim: Active Rab-GTP recruits a range of specific effector proteins to the membrane that mediate key trafficking functions.
source: Active Rab-GTP then recruits a range of specific effector proteins to the membrane that mediate key trafficking functions, including cargo selection, vesicle budding, transport, tethering and fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rab GTPase function.

claim: GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) deactivate Rabs by promoting GTP hydrolysis.
source: Subsequently, GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) deactivate Rabs by promoting GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rab GTPase regulation.

claim: Many membrane compartments have been defined by well-established localized functions of specific Rabs.
source: Many membrane compartments have been defined by well-established localized functions of specific Rabs, for example: ER (Rab1), Golgi (Rab1, Rab6), secretory vesicles (Rab8), early endosomes (Rab5, Rab21), recycling endosomes (Rab11, Rab35), late endosomes (Rab7, Rab9), lysosomes (Rab7) and others (Jean and Kiger, 2012; Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: mCD8:GFP showed a mesh-like pattern in pharate/pre-adult dorsal abdominal IOMs at 4d APF by live imaging.
source: When observed in live IOM persistent larval muscles through the cuticle at 4 days after puparium formation (4d APF), mCD8:GFP showed a mesh-like pattern (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is directly observed in the data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: mCD8:GFP colocalized with Dlg1-marked T-tubules in fixed samples.
source: that in fixed samples colocalized with Dlg1-marked T-tubules (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown by colocalization analysis in the figures.

claim: mCD8:GFP colocalized with sarcomere Z-lines.
source: and sarcomere Z-lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by colocalization analysis in the figure.

claim: The IOMs remodeled during metamorphosis with myofiber thinning through 2d APF followed by rethickening from 3-4d APF.
source: As previously reported (Kuleesha et al., 2014; Wasser et al., 2007), the IOMs remodeled during metamorphosis with myofiber thinning through 2d APF followed by rethickening from 3-4d APF (Figure 1E–F, top and middle rows).
evidence: This is observed in the time course data and cited from previous literature.

claim: Well-organized mCD8:GFP-marked membranes detected in third instar larval precursor muscles were disassembled in IOMs by 1-2d APF and then reassembled by 4d APF.
source: Along with these cell morphology changes, the well-organized mCD8:GFP-marked membranes detected in third instar larval precursor muscles were disassembled in IOMs by 1-2d APF and then reassembled by 4d APF (Figure 1F, middle and bottom rows).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: Dlg1:GFP (T-tubules), Reticulon:GFP (Sarcoplasmic Reticulum; SR), and GFP:actin (myofibrils) were each disassembled by 1-2d APF, and then reassembled by 4d APF in IOMs.
source: To more specifically investigate myofiber remodeling, we monitored Dlg1:GFP (T-tubules), Reticulon:GFP (Sarcoplasmic Reticulum; SR), and GFP:actin (myofibrils) at 24h intervals during metamorphosis (Figure 2A). Each of these organelles was disassembled by 1-2d APF, and then reassembled by 4d APF in IOMs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis of myofiber remodeling by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed both the timing and extent of the disassembly and reassembly stages during metamorphosis.
source: Furthermore, ultrastructual analysis of myofiber remodeling by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging of IOM transverse sections (Figure 2B) confirmed both the timing and extent of the disassembly and reassembly stages during metamorphosis (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: This is observed in the TEM data.

claim: Differentiated myofiber structures critical for muscle function, including T-tubule membranes, undergo regulated and stereotypical remodeling in IOMs during metamorphosis.
source: This reveals that differentiated myofiber structures critical for muscle function, including T-tubule membranes, undergo regulated and stereotypical remodeling in IOMs during metamorphosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time course and TEM data.

claim: A muscle-targeted RNAi screen of 300 candidate membrane trafficking-related genes was performed.
source: In order to identify functions involved in T-tubule membrane remodeling, we performed a muscle-targeted RNAi screen of candidate membrane trafficking-related genes, including all fly genes predicted to encode Rab GTPases, Arf GTPases, sorting nexins, BAR domain proteins, SNARE proteins, and phosphoinositide regulators (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken.

claim: Among 300 RNAi lines tested, 77 lines showed a defect in adult eclosion or mobility.
source: Among 300 RNAi lines tested, 77 lines showed a defect in adult eclosion or mobility, 151 lines resulted in normal viability and mobility, and 83 lines were unscored due to pre-adult lethality (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is the result of the primary screen.

claim: 10 RNAi lines targeting a set of 5 different genes (two Rab GTPases and three SNARE proteins) showed a similar phenotype with accumulation of mCD8:GFP-positive small vesicles.
source: We identified 10 RNAi lines targeting a set of 5 different genes, representing two Rab GTPases and three soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins, with a similar phenotype (Figure 3A–B and Supplementary file 1). Instead of the organized T-tubule network seen in control IOMs, RNAi of Rab2, Rab7, Stx17, SNAP29 or Vamp7/8 each resulted in an accumulation of mCD8:GFP-positive small vesicles that filled often misshapen or swollen myofibers (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is the result of the secondary screen.

claim: T-tubules (Dlg1) and most myofibrils (F-actin) were absent throughout RNAi-treated IOMs at 4d APF for Rab2, Rab7, Stx17, SNAP29, or Vamp7/8.
source: Unlike in controls, T-tubules (Dlg1) and most myofibrils (F-actin) were absent throughout these RNAi-treated IOMs at 4d APF (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: Stx17, SNAP29, and Vamp7/8 form a trans-SNARE complex involved in autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that four of the five genes play known roles together in lysosome fusion: Stx17, SNAP29, and Vamp7/8 form a trans-SNARE complex involved in autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Itakura et al., 2012; Takáts et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Rab7 functions in late endosome-lysosome fusion as well as late steps in autophagy.
source: while Rab7 functions in late endosome-lysosome fusion as well as late steps in autophagy (Gutierrez et al., 2004; Jäger et al., 2004; Hegedűs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Rab2 had been previously implicated with functions at the ER and Golgi.
source: It was unexpected, however, to find a shared RNAi phenotype between this set of known functions and Rab2, which had been implicated with functions at the ER and Golgi (Saraste, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The specificity of the Rab2 RNAi phenotype was confirmed by rescue with co-expression of a wildtype Rab2 transgene.
source: The specificity of the Rab2 RNAi phenotype was confirmed by rescue with co-expression of a wildtype Rab2 transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown by the rescue experiment data.

claim: The HOPS complex mediates SNARE-dependent autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: To explore this possibility, we tested a requirement for the homotypic fusion and protein sorting (HOPS) complex that is known to mediate SNARE-dependent autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Jiang et al., 2014; Takáts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Disruption of the HOPS complex with RNAi of subunits Vps39, Vps18, and Vps11 each phenocopied the specific Rab2 class of IOM defects.
source: As expected, disruption of the HOPS complex with RNAi of subunits, Vps39, Vps18, and Vps11 each phenocopied the specific Rab2 class of IOM defects (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is observed in the RNAi phenotype data.

claim: A defect in autophagosome-lysosome fusion leads to the unique Rab2 class of RNAi phenotypes in IOM remodeling.
source: These results suggest that a defect in autophagosome-lysosome fusion leads to the unique Rab2 class of RNAi phenotypes in IOM remodeling and predicts a novel role for Rab2 in autophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared phenotypes of genes known to function in autophagosome-lysosome fusion.

claim: The mCherry:GFP:Atg8a autophagic flux reporter indicates both dually-labeled Atg8-marked autophagosomes and mCherry-labeled autolysosomes.
source: The mCherry:GFP:Atg8a autophagic flux reporter indicates both dually-labeled Atg8-marked autophagosomes and, due to the greater resistance of mCherry than GFP to lysosomal proteases, the successful delivery of autophagosomes to the lysosome by mCherry-labeled autolysosomes (Kimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from the literature describing the reporter.

claim: In control IOMs, there were dual mCherry-GFP-positive autophagosomes, as well as just mCherry-positive degradative autolysosomes.
source: In control IOMs, there were dual mCherry-GFP-positive autophagosomes, as well as just mCherry-positive degradative autolysosomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: The Rab2, Rab7 and Stx17 RNAi IOMs contained a striking increase in dual mCherry-GFP-positive puncta.
source: In contrast, the Rab2, Rab7 and Stx17 RNAi IOMs contained a striking increase in dual mCherry-GFP-positive puncta (Figure 4A–B), showing that autophagosome clearance was severely blocked either due to accumulation of autophagosomes or nondegradative autolysosomes.
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: Autophagosome clearance was severely blocked in Rab2, Rab7 and Stx17 RNAi IOMs.
source: In contrast, the Rab2, Rab7 and Stx17 RNAi IOMs contained a striking increase in dual mCherry-GFP-positive puncta (Figure 4A–B), showing that autophagosome clearance was severely blocked either due to accumulation of autophagosomes or nondegradative autolysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of dual-positive puncta.

claim: Stx17 localized to the vesicle membranes in the RNAi conditions.
source: In the RNAi conditions, Stx17 localized to the vesicle membranes (Figure 4C) also marked with Atg8 (Figure 4D; 0.53 Pearson correlation), indicating their identity as primarily mature autophagosomes.
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: Stx17-positive vesicle membranes were also marked with Atg8, indicating their identity as primarily mature autophagosomes.
source: In the RNAi conditions, Stx17 localized to the vesicle membranes (Figure 4C) also marked with Atg8 (Figure 4D; 0.53 Pearson correlation), indicating their identity as primarily mature autophagosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data.

claim: TEM myofiber transverse sections revealed Rab2, Rab7 or Stx17 RNAi-depleted IOMs similarly and uniformly filled with thousands of accumulated autophagosomes carrying nondegraded cytoplasm and organelles.
source: Confirming these results, TEM myofiber transverse sections (Figure 2B) revealed Rab2, Rab7 or Stx17 RNAi-depleted IOMs similarly and uniformly filled with thousands of accumulated autophagosomes carrying nondegraded cytoplasm and organelles (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is observed in the TEM data.

claim: Rab2 is required for autophagosome-lysosome fusion with myofiber remodeling.
source: Thus, similar to previous reports of Rab7, Stx17, SNAP29 and Vamp7/8 functions in other Drosophila tissues (Hegedűs et al., 2016; Takáts et al., 2013), with myofiber remodeling, Rab2 also is required for autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotype data and comparison to known functions of other genes.

claim: Muscle-targeted Atg1, Atg3 or Atg18 RNAi resulted in disorganized and fragmented T-tubules and sparse myofibrils in IOMs at 4d APF.
source: We further validated a requirement for autophagy in T-tubule remodeling by disrupting early steps in autophagy with muscle-targeted Atg1, Atg3 or Atg18 RNAi. In each case, RNAi resulted in disorganized and fragmented T-tubules and sparse myofibrils in IOMs at 4d APF (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: TEM analysis of IOMs with Atg1 or Atg18 RNAi showed a lack of T-tubules, disorganized myofibrils and a striking accumulation of mitochondria that filled the cells.
source: Furthermore, TEM analysis of IOMs with Atg1 or Atg18 RNAi showed a lack of T-tubules, disorganized myofibrils and a striking accumulation of mitochondria that filled the cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the TEM data.

claim: Mitochondria are a major cargo of autophagy during IOM remodeling.
source: The accumulation of fluorescently-marked mitochondria (Figure 5D) confirmed the TEM observations of free mitochondria within the cytoplasm with Atg1 RNAi (Figure 5C) or inside mature but blocked autophagosomes with Rab2 RNAi (Figure 4E), suggesting that mitochondria are a major cargo of autophagy during IOM remodeling.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of mitochondria when autophagy is blocked.

claim: Autophagosomes did not occur or accumulate in IOMs with Atg1 and Atg18 RNAi.
source: As expected for a block in autophagy induction, and unlike the Rab2 RNAi, autophagosomes did not occur or accumulate in IOMs with Atg1 and Atg18 RNAi.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of autophagosome markers in the imaging data.

claim: The number of Atg8 puncta indicative of autophagosomes dramatically increased by 1d APF and then sharply decreased by 3d APF in wildtype IOMs.
source: The number of Atg8 puncta indicative of autophagosomes dramatically increased by 1d APF and then sharply decreased by 3d APF (Figure 6A, top row and 6B).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: The number of Lamp1 and Rab7 marked endolysosomes or amphisomes/autolysosomes also increased during pupal stages 1d-3d APF.
source: Likewise, the number of Lamp1 and Rab7 marked endolysosomes or amphisomes/autolysosomes also increased during pupal stages 1d-3d APF (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: The increase in autophagy at 1d APF does not reflect an autophagy role in myofiber cell death.
source: Importantly, the increase in autophagy at 1d APF does not reflect an autophagy role in myofiber cell death, as the IOMs normally survive throughout metamorphosis (Figures 1–2) and assist days later with adult eclosion (Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IOMs survive and function after metamorphosis.

claim: A reproducible onset of autophagy induction occurred between 12h and 18h APF that peaked by 20h APF in IOMs.
source: We quantified a reproducible onset of autophagy induction between 12h and 18h APF that peaked by 20h APF in IOMs (Figure 6C, top row and 6D, red).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: T-tubules remained intact from third instar larval through 12h APF stages, became partially fragmented by 18h APF and were completely absent by 20h APF in wildtype IOMs.
source: In parallel experiments, we used live imaging of a PI(4,5)P2 biosensor to detect T-tubules and the plasma membrane. While the T-tubules remained intact from third instar larval through 12h APF stages, the PI(4,5)P2-marked T-tubule membrane network became partially fragmented by 18h APF and was completely absent by 20h APF in wildtype IOMs (Figure 6C, bottom row and 6D, blue).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: There are highly reproducible, coincident onsets and peak occurrences of both T-tubule disassembly and autophagy induction between 18-20h APF.
source: These results show highly reproducible, coincident onsets and peak occurrences of both T-tubule disassembly and autophagy induction between 18-20h APF (Figure 6C–D), supporting interrelated roles for autophagy and T-tubule remodeling.
evidence: This is observed in the time course data.

claim: Defects in T-tubule remodeling arose within the first day of IOM remodeling in both the Rab2 class and Atg1 class of RNAi phenotypes.
source: Consistent with the timing of autophagy induction in wildtype IOMs (Figure 6D), a timecourse analysis of T-tubule remodeling in both the Rab2 class (Rab2, Rab7 or Stx17) and Atg1 class (Atg1, Atg18 RNAi) of RNAi phenotypes revealed that defects arose within the first day of IOM remodeling (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–2B).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: Normal T-tubule networks were observed in the IOM precursor muscles at the third instar larval stage in all RNAi conditions tested.
source: In all cases, normal T-tubule networks were observed in the IOM precursor muscles at the third instar larval stage (Figure 6E, left), in line with the normal larval mobility observed with each muscle-targeted RNAi depletion.
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: Initial defects in mCD8:GFP organization appeared between 12h and 18h APF in RNAi conditions.
source: However, initial defects in mCD8:GFP organization appeared between 12h and 18h APF (Figure 6E), at a time when normally both T-tubule disassembly and autophagy induction occur (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is observed in the time course imaging data.

claim: Knockdown IOMs remained persistently blocked at an 18–20h stage in remodeling throughout metamorphosis.
source: These knockdown IOMs remained persistently blocked at an 18–20h stage in remodeling throughout metamorphosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the time course data showing no progression beyond the initial defect stage.

claim: In control IOMs at the time of T-tubule disassembly at 18–20h APF, mCD8:GFP-marked membranes reorganized into dispersed bright patches and some vesicles.
source: In control IOMs at the time of T-tubule disassembly at 18–20h APF (Figure 6C–6D), mCD8:GFP-marked membranes reorganized into dispersed bright patches and some vesicles (Figure 6E, top row and Figure 6F).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: In the Rab2 class of RNAi phenotypes, T-tubule disassembly at 18–24h APF occurred in conjunction with an abnormal accumulation of uniformly-sized mCD8:GFP vesicles.
source: In the case of the Rab2 class of RNAi phenotypes, T-tubule disassembly at 18–24h APF occurred in conjunction with an abnormal accumulation of uniformly-sized mCD8:GFP vesicles (Figure 6E, middle row; Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, top rows), many of which were identified as Atg8-marked autophagosomes (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: The Atg1 class of RNAi phenotypes showed normal timing in initial T-tubule membrane disassembly at 18–20h APF, but with abnormally large clusters of bright mCD8:GFP-positive membrane patches.
source: In contrast, the Atg1 class of RNAi phenotypes showed normal timing in initial T-tubule membrane disassembly at 18–20h APF, but with abnormally large clusters of bright mCD8:GFP-positive membrane patches (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: By 1d APF, the bright membrane clusters increased in size to reveal stacked membrane whirls that persisted to 4d APF in Atg1 class RNAi.
source: By 1d APF, the bright membrane clusters increased in size to reveal stacked membrane whirls that persisted to 4d APF (Figure 6E, bottom row; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, bottom row; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data.

claim: Autophagy plays a key role downstream of initiation and membrane scission in T-tubule disassembly for subsequent mobilization of disassembled T-tubule-derived membranes.
source: Together with the lack of T-tubules and autophagosomes in IOMs with autophagy disruption at 4d APF (Figure 5), these results indicate that autophagy plays a key role downstream of initiation and membrane scission in T-tubule disassembly for subsequent mobilization of disassembled T-tubule-derived membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the different phenotypes of autophagy induction versus clearance defects.

claim: All autophagy functions were consistently required by 18–20h APF when both autophagy induction and T-tubule disassembly normally occurs.

claim: Rab2 RNAi increased the amount of both Atg8-marked autophagosomes and uncleared p62 autophagic cargo in third instar larval fat body.

claim: Mammals each have two Rab2 isoforms, Rab2A and 2B.

claim: Rab2A/B_DKO blocks autophagy flux.
